contraindications: Candesartan: pregnancy (second and third trimester fetotoxicity).
Topiramate: pregnancy; in a woman who can become pregnant only with highly effective contraception under the pregnancy prevention programme (MHRA 2024).
output.formulary_status: Candesartan, topiramate: on formulary. Erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab: restricted to NICE technology appraisal criteria (at least 4 migraine days a month and at least 3 failed preventive drug treatments).
interactions: Erenumab with sumatriptan or naproxen: no pharmacokinetic interaction (monoclonal antibody).
Candesartan with naproxen: NSAIDs reduce the antihypertensive effect and, with regular use, raise the risk of renal impairment and hyperkalaemia; occasional use is acceptable.
Topiramate with the levonorgestrel IUS: no loss of contraceptive efficacy (the IUS acts locally); topiramate reduces the efficacy of oral contraceptive pills.
Sumatriptan with candesartan or topiramate: no clinically significant interaction.
output.proposed: Migraine preventive options: erenumab; candesartan; topiramate. Current: sumatriptan, naproxen, levonorgestrel IUS
output.summary: No interaction of erenumab, candesartan or topiramate with sumatriptan or her IUS; candesartan and topiramate need pregnancy safeguards, and NSAIDs blunt candesartan. Sources: SmPCs, BNF, MHRA Drug Safety Update 2024, NICE TA682.
warnings: Erenumab: constipation, sometimes severe; hypertension reported after marketing; injection-site reactions.
Candesartan: hypotension and dizziness at start; check renal function and potassium.
Topiramate: paraesthesia, cognitive slowing, weight loss, kidney stones, rarely acute angle-closure glaucoma.
CGRP monoclonal antibodies: avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding (limited data).

output.query: CGRP monoclonal antibody migraine prevention eligibility after failed oral preventives

results.finding: Erenumab 70 mg and 140 mg monthly reduced monthly migraine days by 3.2 and 3.7 days versus 1.8 with placebo over months 4-6.
results.source: Goadsby PJ et al. A controlled trial of erenumab for episodic migraine (STRIVE). N Engl J Med 2017;377:2123-2132

results.finding: Recommended for adults with at least 4 migraine days a month only after at least 3 preventive drug treatments have failed; stop if monthly migraine days are not reduced by at least 50% after 12 weeks (episodic migraine).
results.source: NICE TA682, Erenumab for preventing migraine (2021); TA659 galcanezumab; TA764 fremanezumab

results.finding: CGRP monoclonal antibodies are effective and well tolerated in episodic and chronic migraine, including in people with previous preventive failures.
results.source: Sacco S et al. European Headache Federation guideline on monoclonal antibodies targeting the CGRP pathway for migraine prevention: 2022 update. J Headache Pain 2022;23:67

results.finding: CGRP monoclonal antibodies are indicated after inability to tolerate, or inadequate response to, a 6-8 week trial of at least 2 established oral preventives.
results.source: Ailani J et al. AHS consensus statement 2021. Headache 2021;61:1021-1039

output.summary: CGRP monoclonal antibodies reduce monthly migraine days in episodic migraine; eligibility follows failed oral preventives (at least 2 in the AHS 2021 statement, at least 3 under NICE technology appraisals) and at least 4 migraine days a month under NICE.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Ten years of identical attacks, now 3-4 severe a month; visual aura spreading over 20-25 minutes then migraine headache, 5 of 6 C characteristics; the episode queried as TIA had the same positive spreading features; two failed preventives; normal examination
action_criteria.label: Take a structured headache/aura history, neurological examination and red-flag review; apply every ICHD-3 1.2 criterion explicitly
action_criteria.rationale: The history decides both questions of the case: the earlier 'TIA' had the features of aura (positive symptoms spreading over minutes, followed by headache), and the attack frequency, disability and previous preventives decide the next preventive step.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy for presumed TIA: the episodes have the features of migraine aura (positive symptoms spreading over minutes, followed by headache, the same features as her usual attacks) and the MRI at the time showed no infarct.
Do not continue or start combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch or ring): migraine with aura is UKMEC category 4; offer a progestogen-only method or an IUD.
Do not offer valproate for migraine prevention: she can become pregnant (MHRA 2024).
required_recommendations: Diagnose migraine with typical aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1) and record that the episode queried as TIA 4 years ago had the features of aura; no further vascular investigation or antithrombotic is needed.

Offer a third oral preventive class now (3-4 severe attacks a month): candesartan 8 mg rising to 16 mg daily, or topiramate titrated to 50 mg twice daily under the pregnancy prevention programme (her levonorgestrel IUS is highly effective contraception); review after 8-12 weeks with a headache diary.

Discuss a CGRP monoclonal antibody (erenumab, fremanezumab or galcanezumab) if the third preventive fails or is not tolerated, as NICE technology appraisals (TA659, TA682, TA764) require at least 3 failed preventives and at least 4 migraine days a month; the EHF 2022 guideline supports their efficacy and long-term safety [Sacco_2022].
Acute plan: sumatriptan 100 mg with naproxen 500 mg at headache onset, prescribed in a quantity that covers her attacks, keeping triptan use under 10 days a month.

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis — neither present here
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura — no role unless cardioembolic stroke is on the differential
EEG is not indicated for migraine with aura; reserve for cases where focal seizure is genuinely on the differential

accepted: Established migraine with typical visual aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1); previous 'TIA query' retrospectively was visual aura

differential.key_features: Excluded as the main diagnosis: every attack has a stereotyped, gradually spreading visual aura
Acute medication on about 4-6 days a month (sumatriptan up to 4, naproxen): below the 10-day triptan threshold; headache is episodic

The queried episode had positive visual symptoms spreading over 20 minutes and was followed by headache, like her usual attacks; no limb or speech deficit; no vascular risk factors; MRI at the time reported normal
Throbbing unilateral headache with nausea and photophobia after an aura is migrainous

key_clinical_evidence: The episode queried as TIA 4 years ago was a 20-minute positive visual disturbance spreading across the field and followed by headache, the same features as her usual aura; the MRI at the time was reported normal.

Three to four severe attacks a month reach the AHS 2021 threshold to offer prevention; propranolol was not tolerated and amitriptyline 25 mg was ineffective and not tolerated, so a third oral class comes before a CGRP antibody under NICE technology appraisals.
Her levonorgestrel IUS is UKMEC 2 in migraine with aura and is highly effective contraception for a topiramate pregnancy prevention programme.

findings.result: Stereotyped attacks for 10 years; 3-4 a month now, up from 1-2 a month three years ago; character unchanged.
Visual only: shimmering crescent-shaped arc, usually in the right visual field, expanding and clearing; fully reversible. No sensory, speech, motor or brainstem symptoms.
Left-sided throbbing headache, 7-8/10, follows the aura; nausea and photophobia; lasts 6-10 hours.

findings.element: Episode queried as TIA 4 years ago
findings.result: Shimmering disturbance spreading across the left visual field over 20 minutes, followed by headache; no limb or speech symptoms. Same positive, spreading character as her usual attacks.

Sumatriptan 100 mg effective, on up to 4 days a month; naproxen 500 mg partial relief; acute-medication days about 4-6 a month. Normal: full visual fields, no papilloedema, normal power, reflexes, sensation, coordination and gait.

patient.history_present_illness:
A 38-year-old British woman with a 10-year history of migraine with typical visual aura presented to the neurology outpatient clinic requesting more effective preventive therapy. She describes classic episodes beginning with a bright crescent-shaped shimmering arc in the right visual field that expands over 20-25 minutes, followed by a left-sided throbbing headache (7-8/10) with nausea and photophobia lasting 6-10 hours. She has 3-4 episodes per month, increased from 1-2 per month three years ago.

She has tried sumatriptan 100 mg (effective but 4 episodes/month exhausts her prescription) and naproxen 500 mg (partial relief). Previous preventive attempts include propranolol 40 mg BID (stopped after 3 months — fatigue and bradycardia), amitriptyline 25 mg (poor effect at this dose, then stopped due to dry mouth). She is interested in newer anti-CGRP treatments after reading about them online.

She has no cardiac disease, no hypertension, and no depression. She had a 'minor TIA' query 4 years ago: on further questioning, this was a 20-minute shimmering disturbance spreading across the left visual field, followed by a headache, without any limb or speech symptoms; it was investigated at the time and the MRI brain was reported as normal. She was not started on any long-term medication afterwards. She is a non-smoker and uses a levonorgestrel intrauterine system for contraception. She would like to discuss erenumab.
